title: Brushed-metal windows in Mac OS X
lede: A second Aqua window style with a brushed-aluminium texture, used for QuickTime Player, iTunes, the Finder, and Safari.
summary: Brushed-aluminium window frames with sunken buttons. Apple, QuickTime 4 (1999) to Mac OS X Leopard (2007).
made: First in QuickTime Player 4 (1999); widest use in Mac OS X Panther (2003); merged into one gray window style in Leopard (2007)

evidence.note: No image was inspected. Based on Wikipedia, which cites Apple’s Human Interface Guidelines and Daring Fireball.

styles.note: A precursor material: a metal texture tied to real devices, before the leather, wood, and paper of 2007–2013.

context: “Brushed-metal windows had a thick frame with a metallic texture or dark-gray background and sunken buttons and inner frames.” “Apple recommended brushed-metal windows for applications that mimic real-world devices (such as iTunes) or are used to interface with such devices (such as iSync).” [Wikipedia: Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_(user_interface)).

“Brushed Metal had first appeared in QuickTime Player 4.” Panther used it more, “especially to the Finder and Safari web browser.” In Leopard, Aqua and brushed-metal windows “obtained the same metal-like, gray look.” [Wikipedia: Aqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aqua_(user_interface)).
Wikipedia links the change to Apple’s industrial design: “In 2003 and 2004, Apple moved to the use of brushed aluminium … The design of Aqua changed accordingly.”
interpretation: Apple’s own rule tied the texture to device-like apps. That is the logic of the later style: the material says what kind of object the app is.

rights.statement: Apple software; copyrighted. No image is stored here.
